title: 05. Retrieval, Hybrid & Reranking: How Does a Search Engine Actually Work?
summary: Imagine you walk into a massive library with 1 million books. You ask the librarian: "Find me every book that talks about 'black holes'." > > A bad librarian opens every book, reads every page, and checks if "black holes" appears.

sections.title: ① Real-World Analogy
sections.body:
> Imagine you walk into a **massive library with 1 million books**. You ask the librarian: *"Find me every book that talks about 'black holes'."*
>
> A **bad librarian** opens every book, reads every page, and checks if "black holes" appears. This takes hours.
>
> A **smart librarian** walks to a special filing cabinet labelled **"Index"**, opens the drawer labelled **B**, and instantly finds a card that says: *"black holes → Books #42, #7891, #234502"*. Done in seconds.
>
> **Search engines are smart librarians.** The "filing cabinet" is called an **inverted index**.

sections.title: ② Plain English Explanation
sections.body:
A search engine has two jobs:
1. **Before you search** — it reads all documents and builds a giant lookup table (the index)
2. **When you search** — it uses that lookup table to instantly find matching documents, then sorts them by *how well* they match your query

The sorting step is called **relevance scoring** — giving each document a number that says "how good of a match is this?"

The document with the highest score goes to position #1. The lowest-scoring document goes last.

sections.title: ③ Why Does This Matter?
sections.body:
**The problem:** If Google had to read every webpage every time someone searched, it would take years per search. The world has trillions of webpages.

**The solution:** Pre-process all documents into an index *once*, then search the index instantly.

**Why scoring matters:** Returning all matching documents is useless if there are 50 million matches. We need to rank them so the *best* matches come first.

sections.title: ④ Step-by-Step Technical Explanation
sections.body:
**Step 1 — You have documents**
```
Document 1: "Python is great for machine learning"
Document 2: "Java is used for enterprise software"
Document 3: "Python and Java are both programming languages"
```

**Step 2 — Tokenise each document**
Split every document into individual words (tokens):
```
Doc 1 tokens: ["python", "is", "great", "for", "machine", "learning"]
Doc 2 tokens: ["java", "is", "used", "for", "enterprise", "software"]
Doc 3 tokens: ["python", "and", "java", "are", "both", "programming", "languages"]
```

**Step 3 — Build the inverted index**
For each word, record which documents contain it:
```
"python"    → [Doc1, Doc3]
"java"      → [Doc2, Doc3]
"is"        → [Doc1, Doc2]
"machine"   → [Doc1]
"learning"  → [Doc1]
"enterprise"→ [Doc2]
```

**Step 4 — User types a query**
```
Query: "python machine learning"
Tokens: ["python", "machine", "learning"]
```

**Step 5 — Look up each token in the index**
```
"python"   → [Doc1, Doc3]
"machine"  → [Doc1]
"learning" → [Doc1]
```

**Step 6 — Score each document**
```
Doc1: matches all 3 query words → HIGH score
Doc3: matches only 1 query word → LOW score
Doc2: matches 0 query words → score = 0
```

**Step 7 — Rank and return top-K**
```
Rank 1: Doc1 (score: high)
Rank 2: Doc3 (score: low)
```

sections.title: ⑤ Beginner-Friendly Code Example
sections.body:
```python
# ============================================================
# LESSON 1: Simple Search Engine Simulation
# ============================================================

# Step 1: Our tiny document collection (we'll use these 5 docs throughout ALL lessons!)
documents = [
    "Python is great for machine learning and data science",        # Doc 0
    "Java is used for enterprise software development",              # Doc 1
    "Python and Java are both popular programming languages",        # Doc 2
    "Machine learning requires lots of data and computation",        # Doc 3
    "Data science uses Python for statistical analysis and modeling" # Doc 4
]

print("=== Our Document Collection ===")
for i, doc in enumerate(documents):
    print(f"Doc {i}: {doc}")

print()

# Step 2: Tokenise — split each document into a list of lowercase words
def tokenise(text):
    # Convert to lowercase so "Python" and "python" are treated the same
    text = text.lower()
    # Split by spaces to get individual words
    words = text.split()
    return words

print("=== Tokenised Documents ===")
tokenised_docs = []
for i, doc in enumerate(documents):
    tokens = tokenise(doc)
    tokenised_docs.append(tokens)
    print(f"Doc {i}: {tokens}")

print()

# Step 3: Build a SIMPLE inverted index
# This is a dictionary: word → list of document IDs that contain it
inverted_index = {}

for doc_id, tokens in enumerate(tokenised_docs):
    for word in tokens:
        # If we haven't seen this word before, create an empty list
        if word not in inverted_index:
            inverted_index[word] = []
        # Add this document ID to the word's list (avoid duplicates)
        if doc_id not in inverted_index[word]:
            inverted_index[word].append(doc_id)

print("=== Inverted Index (first 10 entries) ===")
for word, doc_ids in list(inverted_index.items())[:10]:
    print(f"  '{word}' → Documents {doc_ids}")

print()

# Step 4: Simple search function
def simple_search(query, inverted_index, documents):
    # Tokenise the query the same way we tokenised documents
    query_tokens = tokenise(query)
    print(f"Query: '{query}'")
    print(f"Query tokens: {query_tokens}")
    
    # Count how many query words each document matches
    doc_scores = {}
    
    for token in query_tokens:
        if token in inverted_index:
            # This token exists in our index
            matching_docs = inverted_index[token]
            for doc_id in matching_docs:
                # Give 1 point for each matching query word
                doc_scores[doc_id] = doc_scores.get(doc_id, 0) + 1
    
    # Sort documents by score (highest first)
    ranked_results = sorted(doc_scores.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
    
    print("\n=== Search Results ===")
    for rank, (doc_id, score) in enumerate(ranked_results, 1):
        print(f"Rank {rank}: Doc {doc_id} (score={score}) → '{documents[doc_id]}'")
    
    return ranked_results

# Step 5: Run a search!
print("=== Running a Search ===")
simple_search("python machine learning", inverted_index, documents)
```

**Expected Output:**
```
=== Our Document Collection ===
Doc 0: Python is great for machine learning and data science
Doc 1: Java is used for enterprise software development
Doc 2: Python and Java are both popular programming languages
Doc 3: Machine learning requires lots of data and computation
Doc 4: Data science uses Python for statistical analysis and modeling

=== Tokenised Documents ===
Doc 0: ['python', 'is', 'great', 'for', 'machine', 'learning', 'and', 'data', 'science']
Doc 1: ['java', 'is', 'used', 'for', 'enterprise', 'software', 'development']
Doc 2: ['python', 'and', 'java', 'are', 'both', 'popular', 'programming', 'languages']
Doc 3: ['machine', 'learning', 'requires', 'lots', 'of', 'data', 'and', 'computation']
Doc 4: ['data', 'science', 'uses', 'python', 'for', 'statistical', 'analysis', 'and', 'modeling']

=== Search Results ===
Rank 1: Doc 0 (score=3) → 'Python is great for machine learning and data science'
Rank 2: Doc 3 (score=2) → 'Machine learning requires lots of data and computation'
Rank 3: Doc 2 (score=1) → 'Python and Java are both popular programming languages'
Rank 4: Doc 4 (score=1) → 'Data science uses Python for statistical analysis and modeling'
```

sections.title: ⑥ Common Beginner Mistakes
sections.body:
❌ **Mistake 1:** Thinking search engines read documents every time a search happens
✅ **Fix:** The index is built once. Searches query the index, not the documents directly.

❌ **Mistake 2:** Thinking "more words matched = better result" is always correct
✅ **Fix:** A 10,000-word document will always match more words just by being long. We need smarter scoring (that's TF-IDF and BM25).

❌ **Mistake 3:** Not lowercasing before indexing — "Python" and "python" become two different entries
✅ **Fix:** Always lowercase both documents and queries before processing.

❌ **Mistake 4:** Thinking the index needs to be rebuilt for every new document
✅ **Fix:** Real search engines support incremental indexing — adding new documents without full rebuild.

❌ **Mistake 5:** Assuming more query words = better results
✅ **Fix:** Sometimes a 1-word precise query finds better results than a 10-word vague query.

sections.title: ⑦ Quick Recap
sections.body:
- 🔍 A search engine **pre-builds an inverted index** — a lookup table from words to documents
- ⚡ The index makes search **instant** — no need to read every document every time
- 📊 **Relevance scoring** ranks documents by how well they match the query
- 🔤 **Tokenisation** is step 1 — splitting text into words and lowercasing them
- 🏆 **Top-K results** are returned — the K highest-scoring documents
